tips.title: Three totals carry most of the topic
tips.body: Angles at a **point** add to $360°$. Angles on a **straight line** add to $180°$. Angles in a **triangle** add to $180°$. Almost every missing-angle question is one of these three, sometimes twice over, and knowing which you are using is what the reason asks for.

tips.title: Look for the Z, the F and the C
tips.body: In parallel lines, **alternate** angles make a Z and are equal; **corresponding** angles make an F and are equal; **co-interior** angles make a C and add to $180°$. Tracing the letter with a finger is the quickest way to tell which pair you are looking at.

tips.title: Exterior angles always total 360
tips.body: Whatever the polygon and however many sides, the exterior angles add to $360°$. So each exterior angle of a **regular** $n$-sided polygon is $\dfrac{360}{n}$, and the interior angle is $180°$ minus that. This is usually faster than the $(n - 2) \times 180$ route.

tips.title: Every step needs a reason, in the right words
tips.body: A geometry answer is marked on its reasons as much as its numbers. Write "angles on a straight line add to $180°$", "alternate angles are equal", "angles in a triangle add to $180°$". A number with no reason loses marks even when it is right.

why.matters:
Three totals carry nearly the whole topic: $360°$ at a point, $180°$ on a straight line, $180°$ in a triangle. Everything else — the Z, the F and the C in parallel lines, the angle sum of a polygon — is built from them, which is why the rules are worth knowing as consequences rather than as a list.

The second half is that geometry is marked on its **reasons**. A right answer with no reason scores badly and a chain of named steps scores well, because the reasons are what shows the angle was deduced rather than measured off the diagram.

examples.title: Why a tiled floor is never pentagons
examples.body:
Tiles come as squares, as triangles and as hexagons, and it is not a matter of taste. For a shape to tile with no gaps, a whole number of its corners must fit round a point — and angles at a point add to $360°$.

A regular hexagon's interior angle is $120°$, and $360 \div 120 = 3$, so three meet exactly. A square gives four, a triangle six. A regular pentagon's angle is $108°$, and $360 \div 108 = 3\tfrac{1}{3}$: three leave a $36°$ gap and four will not fit. Nothing above a hexagon works either, because past $120°$ even three is too many.

So the list of regular shapes that tile a floor is exactly three long, and a one-line angle calculation is the whole proof. It is also why a honeycomb is hexagonal rather than pentagonal.

examples.title: Walking round a field is one full turn
examples.body:
The rule that a polygon's exterior angles add to $360°$ whatever its shape looks like something to memorise. Walk it instead.

Set off along one edge of a field and walk right round the boundary. At each corner you turn by the exterior angle, and when you arrive back at the gate you are facing exactly the way you set off — so the turns must add up to one full revolution. That is $360°$, and nothing in the argument used the number of sides or asked for the shape to be regular.

The field in the table has five corners and turns of 60, 100, 75, 65 and 60 degrees, which total $360$. Its interior angles come to $540$, which is $(5-2) \times 180$ — the same fact read the other way round, since each interior angle is $180°$ minus its turn.

examples.title: The hands at half past three are not at a right angle
examples.body:
Ask what angle a clock's hands make at half past three and almost everyone says $90°$. It is $75°$, and the reason is the thing people forget: the hour hand does not wait at the 3 and jump to the 4.

A full turn is $360°$ over twelve hours, so the hour hand moves $30°$ an hour, which is half a degree a minute. By half past three it has left the 3 and travelled $15°$, putting it at $105°$ from the top. The minute hand is at the 6, which is $180°$. The gap is $180 - 105 = 75°$.

The only fact doing any work is that angles at a point add to $360°$, shared out twelve ways. It is worth the thirty seconds because the same slip — treating something that moves continuously as though it moved in steps — is behind a good many wrong answers that have nothing to do with clocks.

visual.alt: A table of the positions of a clock's two hands at five times, showing that at half past three the hour hand has moved to one hundred and five degrees so the angle between them is seventy five and not ninety

steps.title: The three totals
steps.body:
Nearly every missing-angle question rests on three facts.

- **Angles at a point add to $360°$.** A full turn is $360°$, so anything arranged round a single point must use it up exactly.
- **Angles on a straight line add to $180°$.** A straight line is half a turn.
- **Vertically opposite angles are equal.** When two lines cross, the pairs facing each other are the same.

The third follows from the second. If two angles sit on a line either side of a crossing, each is $180°$ minus the angle between them — so the two facing angles must be equal.

**Using them.** In the first figure, three angles sit on the straight line $DA$. Two are known, at $58°$ and $55°$, so

$$x = 180 - 58 - 55 = 67°.$$

In the second, four angles surround a point: two right angles, one of $110°$ and one unknown. Since they add to $360°$,

$$360 - 90 - 90 - 110 = 70°.$$

> Write the reason next to every step. "Angles on a straight line add to $180°$" is what earns the mark, not the arithmetic.

A number on its own, however correct, is worth less than the same number with its reason beside it. That is the single biggest difference between a good geometry answer and an average one.

steps.title: Parallel lines: Z, F and C
steps.body:
When a straight line crosses two **parallel** lines, eight angles appear — and there are only ever **two different sizes** among them.

The arrows on a diagram are what tell you the lines are parallel. Without them you cannot use any of these rules.

Three pairs have names, and each traces a letter.

- **Alternate angles** make a **Z**. They are on **opposite** sides of the crossing line, between the parallels. They are **equal**.
- **Corresponding angles** make an **F**. They are in **matching** positions at the two crossings. They are **equal**.
- **Co-interior angles** make a **C**. They are on the **same** side, between the parallels. They **add to $180°$**.

> Two of the three are equal. Only co-interior angles add up.

Mixing up alternate and co-interior is the most common error in the topic, and tracing the letter with a finger settles it in a second: the Z and the F join equal angles, the C joins a pair that must total $180°$.

**In the diagram**, the angle marked $70°$ is at position $b$. Then:

- $f$ is **corresponding** to it, so $f = 70°$;
- $c$ is **vertically opposite** to it, so $c = 70°$;
- $d$ and $a$ are on the line with it, so both are $110°$;
- $c$ and $e$ are **co-interior**, so $e = 180 - 70 = 110°$.

Every one of the eight is now either $70°$ or $110°$.

steps.title: Triangles and polygons
steps.body:
**Angles in a triangle add to $180°$.** From this comes one more fact worth knowing outright:

> The **exterior angle** of a triangle equals the sum of the two **opposite interior** angles.

For a triangle with angles $50°$, $60°$ and $70°$, the exterior angle at the $70°$ vertex is $110°$, and $50 + 60 = 110$. It works because both quantities are $180°$ minus the same angle.

**For any polygon with $n$ sides:**

$$\text{interior angles add to } (n - 2) \times 180°.$$

The reason is that a polygon splits into $n - 2$ triangles. A pentagon gives $3 \times 180 = 540°$; an octagon gives $6 \times 180 = 1080°$.

**But the exterior angles are simpler.**

$$\text{exterior angles always add to } 360°,$$

for **every** polygon, however many sides. Walking all the way round a shape turns you through one full circle.

**For a regular polygon** — all sides and angles equal — that gives the fastest route of all:

$$\text{each exterior angle} = \frac{360}{n}, \qquad \text{each interior angle} = 180 - \frac{360}{n}.$$

A regular pentagon: exterior $\tfrac{360}{5} = 72°$, interior $108°$. An octagon: $45°$ and $135°$.

**And it runs backwards.** Given an exterior angle of $24°$, the polygon has $\tfrac{360}{24} = 15$ sides.

**A warning.** Dividing $(n - 2) \times 180$ by $n$ only works for a **regular** polygon. In an irregular one the angles still total the same, but they are not equal, so there is nothing to divide.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
Give a reason for every answer, not just a number.

**Part A — the three totals.**

1. Three angles on a straight line are $58°$, $55°$ and $x$. Find $x$.
2. Four angles at a point are $90°$, $110°$, $90°$ and $y$. Find $y$.
3. Two lines cross and one angle is $70°$. Find the other three.

**Part B — parallel lines.**

4. An angle of $70°$ is given. Find the angle **alternate** to it.
5. Find the angle **co-interior** to it.
6. Find the angle **corresponding** to it.

**Part C — polygons.**

7. Find the total of the interior angles of a decagon (10 sides).
8. A regular polygon has an exterior angle of $24°$. How many sides does it have, and what is each interior angle?

For question 8, start from $360$ and divide.

props.title: The reason column is worth as many marks as the answer

visuals.alt: A blank eight-row table with a column for the answer and a column for the reason

check.prompt: A regular polygon has an exterior angle of $24°$. How many sides does it have?
check.solution: Exterior angles always add to $360°$, so the number of sides is $\dfrac{360}{24} = 15$. Its interior angle is $180 - 24 = 156°$.

steps.title: Going deeper: chains of reasoning, and proving the rules
steps.body:
**Longer questions are chains.** You are given one angle at one end of a figure and asked for one at the other, and there is no single rule connecting them. The method is always the same: find an angle you **can**, write it on the diagram with its reason, and look again.

A worked chain, from $b = 70°$ in the parallel-line diagram to the angle $g$:

1. $c = 70°$, vertically opposite angles are equal.
2. $e = 110°$, co-interior angles add to $180°$ (with $c$).
3. $g = 70°$, angles on a straight line add to $180°$ (with $e$).

Three steps, three reasons. Trying to leap from $b$ to $g$ in one move gets the right answer by luck and scores nothing.

**Proving the rules is fair game too.** The angle sum of a triangle can be proved from the parallel-line facts.

Draw a line through the apex of a triangle, parallel to the base. The two angles at the base are now **alternate** to the two outer angles at the apex, so they are equal to them. Those two, together with the apex angle itself, sit on a straight line — and angles on a straight line add to $180°$. So the three angles of the triangle add to $180°$.

That is a complete proof, and it uses exactly the facts from this topic.

**The polygon rule comes from the triangle rule.** Any $n$-sided polygon can be cut into $n - 2$ triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex, so its angles total $(n - 2) \times 180°$.

**And why exterior angles total $360°$:** walk once round the outside of the polygon, turning through each exterior angle as you go. When you return to your starting point, facing the way you began, you have turned through exactly one full circle.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Angles at a **point** add to $360°$.
- Angles on a **straight line** add to $180°$.
- **Vertically opposite** angles are equal.
- Angles in a **triangle** add to $180°$.
- The **exterior angle** of a triangle equals the two opposite interior angles added together.
- **Parallel lines** need arrows on the diagram before any of the rules can be used.
- **Alternate** angles trace a **Z** and are **equal**.
- **Corresponding** angles trace an **F** and are **equal**.
- **Co-interior** angles trace a **C** and add to **$180°$**.
- Interior angles of an $n$-sided polygon total $(n - 2) \times 180°$.
- **Exterior angles always total $360°$**, for every polygon.
- Regular polygon: each exterior angle is $\dfrac{360}{n}$, each interior is $180 - \dfrac{360}{n}$.
- Going backwards: $n = \dfrac{360}{\text{exterior angle}}$.
- Dividing by $n$ only works for a **regular** polygon.
- **Write a reason for every step**, in the mark scheme's wording.

questions.solution: Alternate angles trace a **Z**, sitting on opposite sides of the transversal between the parallel lines, and they are **equal**. Co-interior angles are the pair that add to $180°$.

options: It depends on the number of sides
questions.solution: Walking once round the outside of a polygon turns you through one full circle, so the exterior angles always total $360°$, for every polygon. $(n - 2) \times 180°$ is the total of the **interior** angles.

questions.prompt: Work out the total of the interior angles of a decagon, which has 10 sides. Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: The interior angles of an $n$-sided polygon total $(n - 2) \times 180°$, so for $n = 10$ that is $8 \times 180 = 1440$ degrees.

questions.solution: Exterior angles total $360°$, so the number of sides is $\dfrac{360}{24} = 15$.

questions.prompt: Work out the size of each interior angle of a regular polygon whose exterior angle is $24°$. Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: An interior angle and its exterior angle sit on a straight line, so they add to $180°$. The interior angle is $180 - 24 = 156$ degrees.

questions.prompt: Why can you not find each interior angle of an **irregular** hexagon by working out $720 \div 6$?
options: Its angles are not all the same size
The formula only works for regular triangles
questions.solution: The six interior angles of any hexagon still total $720°$, but in an irregular hexagon they are different sizes, so there is nothing to divide equally. Dividing by $n$ is only valid when every angle is the same, which is what **regular** means.

questions.prompt: A triangle has angles $50°$, $60°$ and $70°$. What is the exterior angle at the $70°$ vertex?
questions.solution: The exterior angle sits on a straight line with the $70°$, so it is $180 - 70 = 110°$. It also equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, $50 + 60 = 110$, which is a useful check.

questions.prompt: Which fact is used to prove that the angles of a triangle add to $180°$?
questions.solution: Draw a line through the apex parallel to the base. The two base angles are **alternate** to the two outer angles at the apex and so are equal to them. Those three angles lie on a straight line, and so add to $180°$.

questions.prompt: In a parallel-line diagram, two angles trace a C shape. What is the correct reason for the relationship between them?
questions.solution: The reason is **co-interior angles add to $180°$**. A C shape means the two angles sit on the same side of the transversal, between the parallel lines. A Z shape would be alternate angles, which are equal.

questions.prompt:
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, making eight angles labelled $a$ to $h$. Angle $b$, at the upper crossing, is $70°$.

(a) Find angles $c$, $e$ and $g$, giving a reason for each step.

(b) Explain why every one of the eight angles must be either $70°$ or $110°$.
questions.solution: For part a, take it one step at a time and name the rule each time. Angle c is alternate to angle b, since the two sit on opposite sides of the transversal between the parallel lines and trace a Z, and alternate angles are equal. So c is seventy degrees. Angle e is co-interior with angle c, since they sit on the same side of the transversal between the parallels and trace a C, and co-interior angles add to one hundred and eighty degrees. So e is one hundred and eighty minus seventy, which is one hundred and ten degrees. Angle g lies on a straight line with angle e, and angles on a straight line add to one hundred and eighty degrees, so g is one hundred and eighty minus one hundred and ten, which is seventy degrees. For part b, the reason there are only two sizes is that the transversal crosses both parallel lines at exactly the same angle, because the lines never converge. At either crossing, four angles are formed by two straight lines, and those four consist of two pairs of vertically opposite angles, which are equal, with each angle and its neighbour lying on a straight line and so adding to one hundred and eighty. That means each crossing produces only two different sizes, and they must add to one hundred and eighty. Since one of them is seventy, the other is one hundred and ten. And because the angle of crossing is identical at the second parallel line, exactly the same two sizes appear there. So all eight angles are either seventy degrees or one hundred and ten degrees.

questions.prompt:
(a) A regular polygon has an exterior angle of $24°$. Work out the number of sides and the size of each interior angle.

(b) Show that the interior angles of this polygon total $(n - 2) \times 180°$, using your answer to part (a).

(c) A student says: "An irregular polygon with the same number of sides has a different interior angle total." Say whether this is right, and explain.
questions.solution: For part a, the exterior angles of any polygon add to three hundred and sixty degrees. In a regular polygon they are all the same size, so the number of sides is three hundred and sixty divided by twenty four, which is fifteen. An interior angle and its exterior angle lie on a straight line, so they add to one hundred and eighty. Each interior angle is therefore one hundred and eighty minus twenty four, which is one hundred and fifty six degrees. For part b, since all fifteen interior angles are one hundred and fifty six degrees, their total is fifteen times one hundred and fifty six, which is two thousand three hundred and forty degrees. Now check this against the formula: n minus two, times one hundred and eighty, with n equal to fifteen, gives thirteen times one hundred and eighty, which is also two thousand three hundred and forty degrees. The two agree, as they must. For part c, the student is wrong. The interior angle total depends only on the number of sides, not on whether the polygon is regular. Any fifteen-sided polygon can be cut into thirteen triangles by drawing diagonals from a single vertex, and each triangle contributes one hundred and eighty degrees, so the total is always two thousand three hundred and forty degrees. What changes in an irregular polygon is how that total is shared out: the individual angles are no longer all one hundred and fifty six degrees. That is exactly why you can only divide the total by n when the polygon is regular.

examTechnique.body:
**Write a reason beside every step.** These questions are marked on the chain of reasoning, and the mark scheme wants the standard wording:

- angles on a straight line add to $180°$
- angles at a point add to $360°$
- vertically opposite angles are equal
- alternate angles are equal
- corresponding angles are equal
- co-interior angles add to $180°$
- angles in a triangle add to $180°$
- base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal

**Work in small steps.** You will rarely get from what you are given to what is asked in one move. Mark each angle you find on the diagram as you go, and the next step usually becomes obvious.

**For parallel lines, trace the letter.** Z is alternate and equal; F is corresponding and equal; C is co-interior and adds to $180°$.

**"Give reasons" means name the rule**, not describe what you did. "Because they are on a line" is weaker than "angles on a straight line add to $180°$".

**For polygons, prefer the exterior route.** Exterior angles always total $360°$, so a regular $n$-gon has exterior angle $\dfrac{360}{n}$ and interior angle $180 - \dfrac{360}{n}$. Going backwards, $n = \dfrac{360}{\text{exterior angle}}$.

**Check your answer looks right.** An angle drawn acute should not come out as $130°$. Diagrams are usually roughly to scale even when they say they are not.
examinerErrors: Giving the right angle with no reason at all.
Writing "because they are opposite" instead of "vertically opposite angles are equal".
Confusing alternate with co-interior, so a pair that should add to $180°$ is made equal.
Using $360°$ for angles on a straight line, or $180°$ for angles at a point.
Saying the interior angles of a polygon add to $360°$; it is the **exterior** angles that do.
Dividing $(n - 2) \times 180$ by $n$ for an irregular polygon, where the angles are not all equal.
Stopping at an intermediate angle instead of the one the question asked for.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer marks each angle on the diagram as it finds it, so the chain of reasoning is visible rather than held in the head. It names the rule for every step in the standard wording the mark scheme uses. On parallel lines it identifies the letter — Z, F or C — before deciding whether the angles are equal or add to one hundred and eighty. On polygons it reaches for the exterior angle route, because three hundred and sixty divided by n is quicker and harder to get wrong than n minus two times one hundred and eighty. And it checks that the final answer is the angle the question asked for, not the useful one it found on the way.
